Understood. I won’t ask for those four items. We’ll treat omitted requirements as unknowns to document, not ask you to reconstruct what you didn’t have.

One blocker: workspace access is still failing during initialization, so I can’t read the PDFs’ contents right now. I won’t claim that the plan below is aligned to their actual tables or diagrams. I can give you a provisional plan from the repository analysis and retests, then reconcile it with the PDFs when their contents are accessible.

Provisional system plan

Goal: a small, testable MotorPH payroll system whose database schema is grounded in your MO-IT107 work. Use the data dictionary and database design as the schema authority once extracted; don’t assume another numbered submission’s schema is yours.

1. Roles and core features
Employee: view own profile, attendance, and payslips; submit leave or overtime requests if those are in scope.
HR: maintain employee records and review attendance or leave information.
Payroll staff: check attendance and compensation inputs, run payroll for a defined period, review results, and produce payslips or reports.
Administrator: manage accounts, roles, and reference data; review audit records.

Keep only the features supported by the actual assignment scope. The repositories contain more features than were consistently wired or tested.

2. Suggested structure
text
Swing/UI
   ↓
Controllers (receive user actions; validate basic requests)
   ↓
Services (employee, attendance, leave, payroll, reporting rules)
   ↓
Repositories (database reads/writes)
   ↓
Relational database

Keep SQL out of Swing event handlers and payroll arithmetic out of UI classes. Prefer small, testable services and repositories, consistent with the stronger separation seen in folders 4, 6, and 9.

3. Conceptual data areas

These are provisional entity concepts, not a replacement for the MO-IT107 dictionary:

Employee and, if present in the design, Department/Position
UserAccount and Role
AttendanceRecord
LeaveRequest and any leave-balance data
OvertimeRequest
PayrollPeriod or PayrollRun
Payroll detail/result, with earnings and deductions represented as required by the dictionary
AuditLog

A likely relationship pattern is one employee to many attendance records and requests; one payroll run to many employee payroll results. Exact names, keys, cardinalities, and required fields must come from the PDFs, not be guessed here.

4. Main workflows

Employee and account maintenance

text
receive form
validate required fields and references
insert or update through repository
record audit event
refresh view

Attendance

text
capture/import attendance row
validate employee, date, and time values
save the row
retrieve only actual records for the selected employee and period
flag invalid or incomplete rows for review

Leave or overtime request, if in scope

text
employee submits request
validate dates, type, and required explanation
save as Pending
authorized reviewer approves or rejects
update request status and any related balance
commit related changes together, or restore the prior state if a write fails

Payroll

text
select approved period
load active employees, compensation inputs, and actual attendance
validate missing or inconsistent data before calculation
calculate earnings using the approved rules
calculate deductions using the approved rules
calculate net pay
save a payroll run and its employee results
display results and generate payslips/reports

The exact pay-period logic, rates, rounding, overtime, holidays, and leave treatment remain unspecified until verified. I won’t infer official formulas from the example repositories.

5. Data integrity and privacy

Use primary/foreign keys and uniqueness constraints defined by the database design. Use prepared queries, hashed passwords, role checks in services—not just hidden buttons—and restrict access to government identifiers and payroll details. Keep an audit trail for important edits, approvals, and payroll runs.

6. QA approach

Build tests from the data dictionary and DFD:

valid and invalid employee/account inputs
missing, malformed, or duplicate attendance
boundary dates and pay periods
leave approval/rejection and failure during multi-file or multi-table updates
payroll with zero, missing, and ordinary attendance
permission checks for employee, HR, payroll, and admin roles
persistence checks after reopening the app

The previous retests showed why this matters: folder 3 misreads quoted commas, folders 4 and 6 can yield empty datasets for mismatched CSVs, folder 8 assumes an employee exists, and folder 9’s leave service has more explicit validation and rollback behavior. These are comparison evidence, not code to copy automatically.

One consolidated OCR request, only if workspace access stays unavailable

Data dictionary: every table and field; type/length; primary and foreign keys; nullability, uniqueness, defaults, constraints, and field descriptions.
Database design: each entity, relationship, cardinality/optional participation, associative entities, and any written assumptions or normalization notes.
Data-flow diagrams: all levels, process names/numbers, external actors, data stores, labeled input/output flows, and how processes connect. For diagrams, describe arrows as source → process/store (flow label) → destination.
Any visible instructor comments, marks, corrections, or approval notes in the PDFs. Mark unreadable items as [illegible]; don’t guess.

A data flow diagram is an effective tool for simulating and understanding the movement of
data inside a system or process. It plays a crucial role in the analysis, design, and
documentation of systems, assisting in ensuring the swift and correct processing and sharing
of data. Your task this week is to create a data flow diagram for the MotorPH Payroll System
Database. To carry out this activity, follow the steps below:

Instructions:
1. Access the following business information:
a. Business Requirement Specification Document for Payroll System

b. MotorPH Existing Business Processes - Payroll
2. Read and examine the information found within the materials.

3. In DrawlO, make a data flow diagram that illustrates how the data flows in the
MotorPH payroll system using the Gene & Sarson notation style.
a. Create the data flow diagram at least until Level 2.
4. Once completed, insert a snapshot of the diagram, fill in the required information in the
template provided below, and delete this section prior to submission.

# `testingester` numbered submissions — structure, behavior, and course links

**Repository reviewed:** `/home/user/repo_review/full_repo/testingester-main/` (export of `Sitramonicus/testingester`). The numbered projects are nested beneath each `N/-/` directory; folder 8 has one more nested copy of its project root. This document records the initial static pass: source layouts, READMEs/setup notes, implementation paths, data-file headers, build metadata, and available test/evidence files. Behavioral testing was subsequently performed from isolated copies; see `/home/user/repo_review/submission-test-results.md` for observed runtime evidence and environment blockers. The test totals cited here as README/log claims were not rerun as part of the static pass. No employee records or passwords are reproduced.

## Folder 1 — SQLite/NetBeans Swing payroll manager

**Location:** `1/-/src/EmployeePayrollMph/`. There are 12 Java source files, many NetBeans `.form` files, images and bundled JARs. `build/classes/` also contains compiled `.class` files and form copies; those are build output, not a second source implementation. The project metadata names `EmployeePayrollMph.EmployeePayrollMph` as its entry point.

**How it works:** the entry frame presents a login form. Its handler queries the SQLite `Users` table using a prepared statement, stores the selected user's ID/name in static fields on `Emp`, records a login event in `EmployeeAudit`, then opens `MainMenu`. The menu opens employee management, allowances, salary update, deductions, payment records, search and audit. The included SQLite database schema has `Employee_info`, `Users`, `Allowance`, `Salary_Deduction`, and `EmployeeAudit` tables.

The `Employee` frame performs employee add/update/delete against `Employee_info`, including an image BLOB. `Allowance` reads an employee, calculates an allowance total, and inserts a row into `Allowance`. `SalaryDeductions` inserts a deduction record. `EmployeeSalary` looks up the employee plus stored allowances/deductions to prepare a payslip; the app bundles iText, and the menu has PDF report export handlers. This is therefore more of a database-backed admin CRUD app than a clean payroll-calculation library.

**Caveats:** the SQLite connector uses a hard-coded Windows path under one developer's `C:\Users\...` directory even though database files are included in the project. Several screens are mainly generated Swing code; `EmployeeAttendance` and `EmployeeLeave` exist, but their presence alone does not establish a complete persisted attendance/leave workflow. The login's role check uses Java string identity (`==`) and contains an empty `if (count == 1);` statement, so the code should not be treated as a reliable authentication example without checking/fixing that flow.

**Course connection:** the code is useful for seeing Swing event handlers, JDBC/SQLite, CRUD and report generation. There is no source evidence tying it to CP1, CP2, MS1 or MS2, so I would not label it as your coursework baseline.

## Folders 2 and 5 — one Swing/MySQL app under two different labels

**Locations:** `2/-/` and `5/-/`. Each has 49 Java files, many NetBeans `.form` layouts and image assets, a Maven file, and two third-party time-picker JARs. The active entry point is `main.main`, which opens `Jframes.LogInNew`; `Archived/` contains four older screens.

**How it works:** the login screen queries the local MySQL `user_accounts` table and routes Admin/IT users to `AdminHomeDashboard`, other users to `HomeDashboard`. The employee dashboard links to profile, salary, attendance, leave requests and overtime requests. The admin side links to employee records, salary/attendance, accounts, leave approvals and overtime approvals. The screens issue SQL directly through `Classes.db`, which connects to a local MySQL database named `motorph`. SQL references tables named `employees`, `user_accounts`, `attendance_records`, `salary`, `leave_requests`, and `overtime_requests`.

There is a `Classes/` package with `Employee`, `Salary`, `Attendance`, `Deduction`, `Payroll`, `UserAuthentication`, `Admin`, `HR`, `Manager`, request and task classes. These communicate the intended domain model, but multiple methods are empty placeholders (for example, model-level payroll/CRUD methods). The working behavior is mostly in Swing-frame event handlers. Salary computation logic appears in both `CreateSalary` and `UpdateSalaryAdmin`, which each query attendance and calculate salary/deductions. This is an example of a GUI-heavy project with some OOP-shaped classes, not a fully separated model/service architecture.

**Important duplication finding:** folders 2 and 5 are not two materially different codebases. A recursive comparison found only four differences: `.DS_Store`, `README.md`, and author-comment lines in `Classes/Employee.java` and `main/main.java`. The executable Java logic, forms, assets and build file otherwise match. Folder 5's README labels it MO-IT103 H1101 Group 1 / CP2; folder 2's README labels it MO-IT110 H2101 Group 3 / OOP. That makes them different submission *packagings/labels*, but essentially the same program. The folder 2 label does not by itself demonstrate that this is your approved MS1 design or your authored work.

**Caveats:** the MySQL schema/setup is not included as a self-contained database export; running requires a local `motorph` database and compatible account setup. Some domain-layer methods are stubs, while substantial behavior is coupled to the UI. The credentials are database-backed, but the source uses direct password comparison; this is not a security design to copy.

**Course connection:** folder 5 is explicitly CP2. Folder 2 is labelled MO-IT110 OOP, but the repository does not include an MS1 design package connecting these classes to an approved design. Treat it as a CP2-style app/OOP comparison unless the mentor confirms more.

## Folder 3 — small CP1/terminal-assessment console exercises

**Location:** `3/-/`. The README identifies a COMPROG1 A1101 Terminal Assessment submission and describes a Phase 1 console payroll system. There are seven Java files, employee CSV/TXT samples, and NetBeans metadata. Six Java files are in package `motorph`; `MotorPH_ReadFromFile.java` is in the default package, so it is a separate runnable entry point.

**How it works:** the files are small, independent demonstrations rather than one integrated app. They show fixed-value examples for hours worked, gross pay and semi-monthly salary; a separate class calculates example deductions; the file-reader program opens `employee_data.csv`, reads salary from a fixed column, applies its own sample deductions, and prints a result. `ComputeGrossPay` has a reusable static multiplication method, while the other examples largely hard-code the employee/time/pay inputs in `main`.

**Caveats:** the README describes a longer planned progression, but the source is still a set of small console programs, not a GUI, database-backed system or connected payroll architecture. The deduction rates differ between files and are explicitly example-style flat rates; they are not a safe source for official payroll rules. The folder's named author is not evidence that the current user authored it.

**Course connection:** this is the clearest CP1/procedural foundation in the numbe
MIDDLE OUTPUT OMITTED
*Two front ends use the data differently:**

- `Console.TACP2` is a terminal workflow: login with employee number/last name; view profile, daily attendance, weekly hours and payroll. It downloads published Google Sheets CSV over HTTP, so it depends on internet access and the sheet schema.
- The Swing UI starts from `GUI.LogIn` and proceeds to `GUI.MainMenu`. It uses the bundled local CSVs and has profile, attendance, payroll, employee table and employee add/update/delete screens.

The `Backend/` package contains employee/attendance records, CSV loading, payroll processors (regular, final-pay and 13th-month variants), statutory deduction calculators, regular/holiday overtime classes, plus leave and payslip-dispute domain classes. The regular payroll processor uses attendance totals and a `Payslip`; deduction types are separate classes. The GUI exposes employee dispute submission and a payroll-side review/resolve/reject frame.

**Caveats:** leave records shown by the GUI are explicitly hard-coded sample rows because there is no leave data file. Payslip disputes live in a singleton in-memory list, not persistent storage, so the records disappear on process exit. The payroll-side dispute frame itself notes role authorization is not implemented. The console path fetches external sheets; the GUI path reads local data—do not confuse them as one identical data flow. This is a CP2-labeled comparison project, not an MS1-approved design by evidence in this folder.

## Folder 9 — documented MO-IT110 Team 3 CP2-to-OOP project

**Location:** `9/-/`. This is the most documented folder: README, old `README.CP2.md`, `SETUP.md`, `oop/NOTES.md`, parity/matrix reports, console/test outputs, a QA workbook, and code. It has 15 Java files in the original GUI `src/`, 13 in `oop/src/` (12 backend classes plus `ConsoleBackendTest`), and 3 test/probe files. The README identifies the OOP work as MO-IT110 OOP Team 3, and identifies the CP2 baseline as MO-IT103 Group 4. Those are source-repository statements, not confirmation of the current user's authorship or reuse permission.

**Two connected source roots:**

- `src/motorphemployee/` is the earlier CP2 Swing app (login, landing screen, dashboard, employee forms, leave screens and related UI). Its data remains in CSV.
- `oop/src/motorphemployee/oop/` is the OOP payroll backend. `Person` → `Employee` → `RegularEmployee`/`ProbationaryEmployee` is the data hierarchy; `GovernmentContributionCalculator` has concrete contribution/tax calculators; `AttendanceLog` models attendance; `PayrollCalculator` coordinates employee + attendance + calculators and produces `PayrollRecord`.
- `ConsoleBackendTest` provides a console test harness before GUI integration. The GUI's `MainMenu`/`Dashboard` were rewired to call the OOP backend rather than compute payroll themselves.
- `AttendanceRepository` loads the real timecard CSV and supplies worked-day data to the payroll flow. `LeaveService` processes approval/rejection and writes the related CSV files; `LeaveForm` still has a separate direct append path noted as an open issue.

**How the feature sequence works:** employee/attendance CSV → `AttendanceRepository`/`AttendanceLog` → `PayrollCalculator` → contribution calculators → immutable `PayrollRecord` → GUI display. The README and notes describe preserving the CP2 UI while replacing duplicated calculations with one backend. They also document changes to modal popups, attendance sourcing and the add-employee form; these are later implementation refinements beyond the core OOP concept demonstration.

**The explicit module link:** the README maps W2 to encapsulation, W3 to abstraction, W4 to inheritance and W5 to polymorphism, and describes MS1 as 16 unique classes, 35 CRC rows and 97 method rows. It says MS2 implements 12 of the 16 design classes; `Credentials`, `LeaveRequest`, `LeaveManagement` and `HRManager` remain design-only. It states the GUI should present only, payroll math should live in the backend, and backend console tests should precede GUI integration. The repo includes official-matrix verification and CP2-parity evidence; the README says some deduction results intentionally differ from CP2 because the OOP version follows the official matrices, while gross pay matches the CP2 baseline. Do not transfer those tax/contribution assumptions to your assignment without checking its current approved rules.

The README reports 91/91 backend checks and several other dated test/GUI evidence logs. I have not rerun them. The QA workbook in this folder is named for a CP2 Group 4 QA submission; it should not be mistaken for proof that the OOP source was authored by the current user.

**Course connection:** the strongest visible MS1→MS2 teaching example in the repository because its own README and code comments map the OOP concepts and design artifacts into implementation. It is useful for studying the mapping, not automatically reusable submission material.

## How these projects relate to the course modules

There are two levels of evidence, and they should not be conflated:

1. **Explicit labels in the files:** folder 3 says COMPROG1/Terminal Assessment; folders 4, 5 and 8 are CP2-labeled or path-identified; folders 6 and 9 explicitly describe MO-IT110 MS2/OOP work; folder 2 is labelled MO-IT110 OOP but lacks an included MS1 package tying its classes to an approved design.
2. **Conceptual fit:** CSV and database folders illustrate data/file I/O; Swing folders illustrate GUI event handling; model/service/backend folders illustrate OOP decomposition; folders 6 and 9 demonstrate inheritance/abstraction/polymorphism; tests and comparison reports illustrate verification.

From the MO-IT110 Modules 02–09 handout previously reviewed, the project focus is the MotorPH payroll application and its employee/attendance data; the handout does **not** prescribe one particular MotorPH spreadsheet tab as the project base. The numbered folders themselves generally do not record a reliable one-to-one mapping from a particular feature to a specific module number. For that reason this report maps folders to the explicit milestones/concepts above rather than inventing claims like “folder 4 is Module 6.” The clearest official milestone relationship is folder 9's stated MS1 design → MS2 implementation, with folder 6 as a separate MS2 example.

| Course concept / deliverable | Where it is visible | How to read the connection |
|---|---|---|
| Procedural foundations, arithmetic, conditions and basic file reading | Folder 3 | Small independent console exercises; useful prior-learning material, not a CP2 baseline. |
| GUI screens, event handlers, employee records and data persistence | Folders 1, 2/5, 4, 7, 8 and 9's original `src/` | Different implementations and storage choices; presence does not imply OOP design compliance. |
| CSV/database input and output | SQLite in 1; MySQL in 2/5; CSV in 3/4/6/7/8/9 | Shows data-source variety. The course brief/module instructions still take precedence over old project choices. |
| Separation of UI from payroll logic | Most clearly 4, 6 and 9; partially 7/8 | Compare real call paths, not package names alone. Folders 6/9 explicitly describe a backend/UI split. |
| Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism | Models in 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9; explicitly week-mapped in 9 | For the user's MS1, the approved design artifacts and rubric—not an old implementation's class list—are authoritative. |
| MS1 OOP Design Package (CRC cards, method dictionary, architecture overview) | Folder 9's README describes its own package; folder 6 refers to an approved design | These are other teams' records. Do not copy/adapt as your own without mentor confirmation and permission. |
| MS2 implementation and tests | Folders 6 and 9 explicitly; folder 9 has the clearest audit trail | Useful to understand how design becomes code; check current assignment rules and authorship first. |
| Terminal Assessment / final QA and documentation | Folder 3's README calls itself a Terminal Assessment; folder 9 reports TA work still open | These labels differ in course/phase and should not be treated as the same assignment. |

## Cross-folder conclusions and safe study order

- **Folders 2 and 5 are the same practical implementation** despite their different README labels; study one, not both, unless comparing the packaging/attribution differences.
- **Folders 4, 5 and 8 are alternative CP2-style systems**, not evidence of the user's personal CP2 app. Their persistence choices differ (CSV vs MySQL vs CSV/online sheet), and their features are not interchangeable.
- **Folder 9 is the best source here for tracing explicit MS1 concepts into MS2 code**, while folder 6 is a smaller, separate implementation example of the same design-to-implementation idea. Both need authorship/permission confirmation before graded use.
- **Folder 3 is a separate CP1-style reference**, not proof that the user has a CP2 app.
- **Folders 1 and 7 have unclear provenance/course stage.** Use them only as generic technical comparisons until a mentor or repository author confirms their context.

Suggested reading order for understanding—not copying—is: **3** (small console building blocks) → **one CP2 project** (4, 5 or 8; folder 4 is the clearest package-separated example) → **6** (smaller MS2 separation) → **9** (most explicit MS1-to-MS2 mapping and evidence). For your own MS1, start from the official rubric and your actual approved project requirements; use another folder only as a comparison after confirming permission and fit.

## Review boundary

This is a static repository explanation, not a correctness audit or a claim that every advertised feature runs. I read source and metadata but did not execute the projects. Several folders have external setup/data dependencies; exact runtime behavior and payroll-rule correctness require separate, course-specific validation. The repository remains unchanged; this report is the only new deliverable.

# Behavioral test results — numbered submissions 1–9

**Purpose:** companion to [`submission-folder-analysis.md`](submission-folder-analysis.md). This document records the initial test pass. The previously blocked/incompatible cases were then re-tested under prepared runtime conditions; see [`submission-retest-addendum.md`](submission-retest-addendum.md) for the current results and the isolated-copy adaptations. No original repository source was edited. All runs that could write data used isolated copies; the uploaded inventory CSV was copied and kept unchanged. No employee names, credentials, or raw payroll rows are reproduced here.

## Executive summary

- **Best verified MS2 evidence:** folders **6 and 9**. Folder 6's bundled backend suite passed **167/167** checks. Folder 9 passed **91/91** payroll/backend checks, **33/33** attendance checks, and **44/44** leave checks (**168 checks total**) when run with `Asia/Shanghai`, matching the user's local timezone. A first folder 9 run under the sandbox's UTC default was **90/91** because the test compared `LocalDate.now()` in UTC with code using `Asia/Manila`; setting the JVM timezone to Asia/Shanghai or Manila made it pass.
- **Important real input defect:** folder 3's bundled employee CSV run completed, but **all 34 reported gross-pay values differed** from the salary column at index 17 when that CSV was parsed correctly. Its reader uses plain `String.split(",")`; every row has a quoted address containing a comma, shifting the assumed field positions. The selected inventory CSV also crashes this reader with `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
- **Inventory CSV compatibility is poor by design**: the selected file has 49 records and five inventory fields, not employee/payroll/attendance fields. Folder 4 and 6 returned empty datasets for incompatible roles; folder 7 padded its 49 rows then failed during employee mapping; folder 8's production loader hit a `NullPointerException`; folder 9's attendance repository rejected the header with an `IOException`. Folders 1, 2, and 5 have no CSV input path to test.
- **Environment blockers:** OpenJDK 11 only, Maven unavailable, no GUI display, and no local MySQL server on port 3306. This prevented full integrated GUI/database testing for several folders. These are distinguished below from defects observed in executable code.

## Test conditions and interpretation

- The uploaded inventory CSV is used **only as the user's requested cross-app compatibility/adversarial input**, not as payroll data. A payroll application not accepting it is not by itself a payroll defect; silent empty data, unchecked exceptions, or misleading success are recorded as observed error-handling behavior.
- “Passed” means the named executable/test returned success or its explicit checks passed. It does not establish that payroll formulas conform to a current official MotorPH specification; no external approved formula oracle was provided.
- “Observed” is based on a run. “Source-backed inference” is a conclusion from inspected code that could not be executed. “Blocked” means unavailable under the current runtime/GUI/database setup.

## Folder-by-folder observations

### Folder 1 — SQLite Swing CRUD

**Observed:** The sources compile with a matching NetBeans `AbsoluteLayout` library supplied only on the test classpath. The bundled SQLite file is populated. The GUI entry point cannot be meaningfully exercised in this headless environment; startup reaches a Swing `HeadlessException`.

**Data flow:** SQLite is the persistent store; UI actions issue database work and populate UI fields/tables. The read-only table counts confirm the database is not an empty placeholder. The source's hard-coded Windows database path is a portability risk, but its behavior against the supplied database path was not tested end-to-end here.

**Limit:** No CSV interface. The test does not verify CRUD integrity, authentication, or payroll calculations through the UI.

### Folder 2 — MySQL Swing application

**Blocked:** Its Maven metadata targets Java 21; this environment has Java 11 and no Maven. No MySQL listener exists on localhost:3306, and Swing cannot be displayed. There are no bundled CSV fixtures to substitute. Do not interpret the lack of runtime results as proof that its SQL flows fail.

**Source-backed inference:** UI event handlers issue SQL through the DB helper; model classes include incomplete/stub methods and salary calculations are duplicated in GUI code. Folder 5 is nearly the same implementation, so the two should not be treated as independent design evidence without confirming their provenance.

### Folder 3 — procedural console calculations and CSV reader

**Observed:** `CalculateHoursWorked`, `ComputeGrossPay`, `ComputeSemiMonthlySalary`, and `MotorPH_ApplyDeductions` all exited 0 on their built-in examples. The bundled `MotorPH_ReadFromFile` processed 34 rows without an exception.

**Observed defect:** The reader's naive comma split is not quote-aware. Every bundled row contains a comma in the quoted address cell. Comparing its 34 printed gross-pay outputs with the correctly parsed CSV salary column at index 17 produced **0 matching values out of 34**. Thus an exit code of zero is not evidence of correct field selection or payroll output.

**Inventory test:** Replacing the expected input with the five-column inventory file caused `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. This is a schema assumption/validation failure, not a payroll formula result.

**Data flow:** Each run reads CSV lines into arrays and calculates/prints values in process memory; no durable payroll result store was exercised.

### Folder 4 — layered Swing/CSV CP2 application

**Observed:** The main `DataRepository`/model/processor subset compiled with the project's Commons CSV 1.9.0 dependency and loaded **35 employee rows** and **5,168 attendance rows** from bundled data. An isolated probe substituting the inventory file returned 0 employees when used as employee data and 0 attendance rows when used as attendance data.

Maven is absent; the full source/test build was not completed. Therefore repository loading was exercised, but service/controller/GUI integration was not.

**Data flow:** CSV rows are parsed into `Employee` and `AttendanceRecord` collections by `DataRepository`; payroll services operate on those objects and other services write CSV. The inventory probe suggests incompatible header/column names result in empty lists rather than a clear schema error. This risks a blan

## What changed—and what did not

**Temporary test-copy adaptations:**

- Folder 1: SQLite URL redirected to the copied database; a synthetic login row was added to the copied database.
- Folders 2 and 5: local database URL/user settings changed in the copied `Classes/db.java`; synthetic schema/data was created in the disposable MariaDB database. The dashboard needed a `profilePicturePath` column, which was added to that test schema after the first login exposed the missing column.
- Folder 4: only two test-helper Java files were adjusted to compile against the production API; image resources were placed in the requested classpath location; the copied credentials CSV was replaced with synthetic QA credentials.
- Folders 3 and 7: only copied CSV fixtures were adapted to match their stated layouts. No payroll calculation/parser source was fixed.
- Other folders: no application source edits were needed for these retests.

**Not changed:** original repository files, original fixtures, and the uploaded inventory CSV. The test adaptations are not proposed product fixes and should not be copied into any candidate submission without separate review.

## Updated interpretation

The earlier setup blockers for Java version, Maven, and headless Swing were removable: supported JDK 21/Maven builds and GUI smoke flows now work for the previously blocked projects. Folder 2 and 5 additionally require a database; their navigation works against the disposable MariaDB schema, but native MySQL-specific differences and actual CRUD/payroll writes remain unverified. Folder 4's manual tests and GUI can run once its test harness/resource layout is accommodated, but Maven itself still runs **zero automated assertions**.

The inventory outcomes remain useful robustness evidence, not valid payroll baselines. On correct-format data, folders 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, and 9 now reach representative application screens; folder 6's suite remains clean; folder 3 works on a simple compatible row but misreads its own bundled CSV because of quoted commas. No failure was hidden by changing production code.

## Remaining focused checks

1. For folders 2 and 5, repeat against the intended MySQL version and a schema confirmed by the mentor; exercise salary creation/update and leave/overtime writes, then verify persistence and rollback/error cases.
2. For folder 4, add real automated assertions only if authorized; validate payroll against the approved rubric. Fixing its resource-path case mismatch would require a separate code-change decision.
3. For folders 1, 6–9, use controlled GUI actions to verify representative writes/exports, not just login/navigation. Keep them on isolated copies.
4. Preserve the folder 3 quoted-comma finding and test boundary rows (empty/zero/negative rates and truncated records) separately; do not “fix” the parser in the analysis copy before measuring the original behavior.
5. Before adopting code from any numbered repository, confirm authorship, assignment fit, and reuse permission with the mentor.

1.​   Database Overview
      The MotorPH Payroll System database is built in a way to allow users to automate,
      organise, and streamline MotorPH payroll processes systematically to provide the
      prerogative of having minimal struggle in handling the payroll operations so that users
      may allocate efforts unto more substantially demanding tasks. Through the
      centralisation of most payroll-related data into a singular, secure, and scalable
      repository, the system facilitates rapid data retrieval and processing, which becomes
      indispensable for timely salary computations, tax management, and adherence to legal
      contributions and compliance. Thus, for this instance, we deliver an expectation that
      this database will not just bring about changes in improvement with data derivation
      and the alleviation of unnecessary exertion but also an effective means through which
      future growth of the organisation may be facilitated at incorporation through adaptive
      mechanisms for data expansion.
         1.​ Employee Management – Captures, updates, and maintains employee records,
             including employment status, department affiliation, salary structure, and
             personal information; this module serves as the primary reference for all
             modules, with nearly every module being eventually tied back to this module’s
             unique identifier.
         2.​ Payroll Processing – Automates payroll computation, taking into account
             attendance records, salary adjustments, overtime hours, tax deductions, and
             government-mandated contributions (SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG, Withholding
             Tax). The system ensures accuracy in salary computation as it does so
             simultaneously       with   the   updating     data,   and furthermore, provides a
             semi-monthly payslip for each employee and a monthly summary for each
             payroll processing cycle.
         3.​ Attendance and Leave Tracking – Integrates with an employee attendance
             logging system to automatically fetch clock-in and clock-out data, whilst
             recording and cataloguing leave applications, ensuring that payroll calculations
             incorporate approved absences, accounts for your active work presence during
             holidays and rest days, and determine applicable leave benefits.
         4.​ Government Contributions and Compliance – Calculates and maintains records
             of   statutory   government-related          organisational   contributions,   including
             employer-employee deductions for government agencies, as mentioned prior.
             The system automatically generates tax reports and government contribution
             summaries to assist in compliance with regulatory bodies.
         5.​ Security and Access Control - Among the features are that the system ensures
             role-based access control (RBAC) for different user levels, restricting

# Retest addendum — supported inputs and prepared runtime

This addendum updates the first-pass findings in [`submission-test-results.md`](submission-test-results.md). It addresses the user's request to retest unvalidated cases using each app's expected interface, and to make temporary adaptations where needed.

## Safety and test setup

- Fresh copies of folders 1–9 are under `/home/user/repo_review/test_runs/compat_retest/`. The source export at `/home/user/repo_review/full_repo/testingester-main/` and the uploaded inventory file were not modified.
- A Java 21 JDK, Maven, and Xvfb were provisioned for the retest. A disposable MariaDB 11.8.6 server and synthetic schema/data were used for folders 2 and 5; that server has been stopped. This is a **MySQL-protocol compatibility test**, not proof against a native MySQL server/version.
- Temporary source/config edits were confined to the fresh test copies and were limited to connection paths/settings or test-harness compatibility. Test fixture rows contain synthetic QA values. Product behavior findings below distinguish these setup changes from application-source defects.
- The inventory CSV remains a deliberate wrong-schema probe. For functional checks, I used bundled fixtures or synthetic data matching each program's interface.

## What changed—and what did not

**Temporary test-copy adaptations:**

- Folder 1: SQLite URL redirected to the copied database; a synthetic login row was added to the copied database.
- Folders 2 and 5: local database URL/user settings changed in the copied `Classes/db.java`; synthetic schema/data was created in the disposable MariaDB database. The dashboard needed a `profilePicturePath` column, which was added to that test schema after the first login exposed the missing column.
- Folder 4: only two test-helper Java files were adjusted to compile against the production API; image resources were placed in the requested classpath location; the copied credentials CSV was replaced with synthetic QA credentials.
- Folders 3 and 7: only copied CSV fixtures were adapted to match their stated layouts. No payroll calculation/parser source was fixed.
- Other folders: no application source edits were needed for these retests.

**Not changed:** original repository files, original fixtures, and the uploaded inventory CSV. The test adaptations are not proposed product fixes and should not be copied into any candidate submission without separate review.

## Updated interpretation

The earlier setup blockers for Java version, Maven, and headless Swing were removable: supported JDK 21/Maven builds and GUI smoke flows now work for the previously blocked projects. Folder 2 and 5 additionally require a database; their navigation works against the disposable MariaDB schema, but native MySQL-specific differences and actual CRUD/payroll writes remain unverified. Folder 4's manual tests and GUI can run once its test harness/resource layout is accommodated, but Maven itself still runs **zero automated assertions**.

The inventory outcomes remain useful robustness evidence, not valid payroll baselines. On correct-format data, folders 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, and 9 now reach representative application screens; folder 6's suite remains clean; folder 3 works on a simple compatible row but misreads its own bundled CSV because of quoted commas. No failure was hidden by changing production code.

## Remaining focused checks

1. For folders 2 and 5, repeat against the intended MySQL version and a schema confirmed by the mentor; exercise salary creation/update and leave/overtime writes, then verify persistence and rollback/error cases.
2. For folder 4, add real automated assertions only if authorized; validate payroll against the approved rubric. Fixing its resource-path case mismatch would require a separate code-change decision.
3. For folders 1, 6–9, use controlled GUI actions to verify representative writes/exports, not just login/navigation. Keep them on isolated copies.
4. Preserve the folder 3 quoted-comma finding and test boundary rows (empty/zero/negative rates and truncated records) separately; do not “fix” the parser in the analysis copy before measuring the original behavior.
5. Before adopting code from any numbered repository, confirm authorship, assignment fit, and reuse permission with the mentor.

## Appendix D — Feature-by-feature pseudocode for folders 1–9


**Cross-cutting acceptance criteria proposed:** no unapproved access to PII; dual approval where the database-design statement applies; auditable create/update/approve/finalize actions; atomic and repeatable payroll runs; correct effective-date/rule version reproduction; no silent acceptance of incompatible input schemas; clear errors rather than empty “success”; tested backup/restore; and no original fixtures altered in test workflows.

## What the nine repositories can—and cannot—contribute to this plan

The nine submissions are comparison material, not verified mappings to the MO-IT107 documents. Their provenance, assignment fit, authorship and reuse permission are not established for the current user. The most relevant technical patterns are: F4's CSV/repository/service separation; F6's OOP payroll refactor and 167-check suite; F9's GUI-to-backend split and strongest documented MS1→MS2 trace; F1/F2/F5's database-backed screens; and F3's small procedural demonstrations. F7/F8 illustrate CSV-driven GUI/backend flows. None should be treated as a definitive MotorPH business-rule source. F2/F5 are near-duplicates. The full repository-by-repository analysis and feature pseudocode are appended below.

## Explicit unresolved inputs (recorded as unknown, not requested again)

- Approved gross-pay, overtime, undertime, holiday/rest-day, paid-leave, deduction, contribution, tax and rounding rules; authoritative values and effective dates.
- Attendance device/import source, schedules, time zone, grace periods, duplicate/missing punches, overnight shifts and correction approval.
- Leave types, accrual frequency/rates/caps, carry-over, negative balance, approver, monetisation and payroll treatment.
- Pay-cycle calendar and semi-monthly period boundaries, proration, eligibility, final-pay treatment, corrections/reversals and rerun behavior.
- Exact employee/supervisor/HR/payroll/admin permissions, team scoping, PII field visibility, dual-approval roles and emergency access.
- Confirmed archive retention, cold-storage format, legal holds, restore/deletion authorization and applicable compliance requirements.
- Which of the nine repositories (if any) is the user's approved baseline and whether any source is authorized for adaptation.
- The two business-reference documents cited by the DFD; they were not supplied and the user does not have them.

These are blockers to claiming policy correctness, not questions repeated to the user. The current plan remains useful as a provisional architecture and gap register.

You’re right—I misunderstood “it” as the report. I’ve now rechecked the three source PDFs: the 25-page database design, the 28-page data dictionary, and the 6-page DFD. The PDFs are accessible. The DFD has little extractable text, so I reviewed its rendered diagrams as well.

Their main points are:

Database design: describes employee management, payroll, attendance and leave, government contributions, and access control. It defines 30 tables and states that access to PII requires approval from two authorized people.
Data dictionary: lists 29 tables and documents their fields, types, constraints, and relationships.
DFD: shows Employee, Supervisor, HR, Payroll Staff, and System Admin interacting with the system. Its flows cover employee management, schedule/time tracking, payroll processing, payslips and monthly summaries, and archival. The diagram labels one-year retention for several logs and two years for payslips; those are document annotations, not confirmed retention requirements.

The design PDFs disagree on several schema details—including employee department/government links, address region, supervisor department, rest-day modeling, and whether leave directly links to a schedule. The DFD also cites two business-reference documents that weren’t supplied. These findings are in the report, clearly separated from proposed assumptions.

submission-comprehensive-report.md
MD

I’ve synthesized the PDFs as one proposed system: maintain employee and schedule data → record attendance and leave → validate payroll inputs and adjustments → calculate and verify payroll → distribute payslips and monthly summaries → archive older records. The database design describes the data, the dictionary defines its fields and constraints, and the DFD shows who handles each step and how records move.

The diagrams add important details beyond the extracted text:

DFD, page 2: shows Employee, Supervisor, HR, Payroll Staff, and System Admin around the system. The arrows distinguish inputs—such as time-in/out, attendance adjustments, leave requests, and payroll updates—from views such as employee information and payslips. PII access is marked as approval-dependent, but the picture doesn’t define a complete permission matrix.
DFD, page 3: groups the flow into Employee Management, Payroll Processing, and Archival, with stores for the Employee Repository, Logs, Payroll, and Cold Storage.
DFD, page 4: breaks employee management into employee-information handling, schedule/time tracking, and government-information access. It separately depicts address, job-profile, PII, attendance, leave, and changelog stores.
DFD, page 5: shows the payroll sequence: timesheet validation; leave monetisation; wage and adjustments; government deductions; basic computation; payslip distribution; monthly-summary compilation. It identifies attendance/leave logs, wage, benefits/deductions, rates, payslips, and summary stores—but not the calculation rules or approved values.
DFD, page 6: depicts appending records to cold storage, then deleting relevant source records. The small “1YO/2YO” labels appear to mean one- and two-year-old records, but the notation is ambiguous. Those arrows describe a proposed process, not verified retention authority.
Database-design schema image, page 5: shows the table relationships and a color legend for access patterns. Government is red, which the legend marks as requiring additional security. The image also exposes inconsistencies with the surrounding prose: it shows Address.regionID, Supervisor.departmentID, Leave.scheduleID, and Schedule.restDayID linked to a separate Rest Day table. Some of these conflict with the detailed table descriptions.
Data-dictionary images: I checked these too; they present table and field definitions, rather than another workflow diagram.

One correction to my earlier summary: the database design includes a Rates.implementationYear field, although the data dictionary omits it. That still doesn’t establish a complete effective-dated history: the Tax Table lacks a validity period, and the meaning and constraints of the implementation-year field need clarification.

Taken together, the images and text describe a role-based payroll system with audit and sensitive-data controls, but they don’t resolve the schema conflicts, detailed permissions, actual payroll/attendance rules, or archival policy. I’ve updated the comprehensive report with the visual findings and corrected rate-field note.

## 16. Cross-document discrepancies and unresolved design questions

The documents are complementary but not fully harmonised. This section is critical for any agent using the synthesis to answer design questions, revise the schema, generate SQL, or evaluate whether the diagrams match the table definitions.

### 16.1 Highest-impact reconciliation questions

For actual implementation or formal correction, the following questions have the largest effect on table structure and referential integrity:

1. **Rest Day:** Should `Schedule` store a `SET` of weekdays, or should it store `restDayID` referencing a separate `Rest Day` record with seven Boolean flags?
2. **Employee–Government relationship:** Should `Government.employeeID` be the sole FK for the 1:1 association, or should `Employee.governmentID` also exist?
3. **Department placement:** Is department assignment stored directly in Employee, derived exclusively through Position, or duplicated in both places?
4. **Address–Region relationship:** Is `Address.regionID` a stored FK, or should region be derived through `Address.cityID` → `Cities.regionID`?
5. **Supervisor department:** Is `Supervisor.departmentID` required in the physical table?
6. **Leave scheduling:** Should `Leave.scheduleID` be present as in the Data Dictionary and ERD?
7. **Rates versioning:** Is `implementationYear` the primary key for Rates, and if so, why does the table constraint section say no PK?
8. **Composite keys:** Should `Government Deductibles` and `Government Tally` use the composite keys shown in the Database Design/ERD?
9. **Holiday uniqueness:** Should the uniqueness rule apply separately to name and date, or only to the combined name/date pair?
10. **Missing FK declarations:** Should `Payroll.monthID`, `LeaveMonetisation.leaveType`, and the region/rest-day links be added to the written FK list and relationship matrix?

A receiving agent should treat these as open specification issues, not as permission to choose whichever implementation seems most convenient.

## 17. What the documents do not specify

This section separates the system's documented elements from details that are absent in the three PDFs. It is especially important for preventing a downstream agent from filling gaps with generic payroll-system assumptions.

### 17.1 No full SQL implementation specification

The documents provide logical column definitions and constraints, but do not identify:

- the target database management system or SQL dialect;
- complete `CREATE TABLE` statements;
- exact enum members for employment status, leave type, leave status, day type, transaction type, contributor, month, accrual frequency, or changelog data type;
- cascade rules for update or delete;
- nullability for every column not explicitly constrained;
- indexes beyond keys and unique rules that are stated;
- generated/identity/auto-increment behaviour for IDs;
- default values other than those explicitly stated for certain timestamps; or
- physical storage, partitioning, replication, or backup configuration.

### 17.2 No payroll formulas

The documents identify components and process names, but do not provide complete formulas for:

- gross income;
- net pay;
- hourly, daily, or monthly salary conversion;
- ordinary overtime;
- holiday overtime;
- holiday pay;
- rest-day pay;
- paid time off compensation;
- undertime;
- benefits totals;
- deduction totals;
- withholding tax;
- SSS, PhilHealth, or Pag-ibig contributions;
- employer versus employee contribution shares;
- government disbursement totals; or
- employee/employer disbursement totals.

The schema provides fields where amounts are stored. The DFD identifies which processes use those amounts. Neither gives the arithmetic rules.

### 17.3 No actual rate schedules or tax brackets

The `Rates` and `Tax Table` tables define the places where rates and brackets are held. The PDFs do not provide actual statutory percentages, amounts, income thresholds, bracket widths, tax formulas, effective dates, or the date on which rate changes take effect.

### 17.4 No complete business rules for leave

The data model provides leave categories, accrual frequency, accrual rate, maximum accrual, leave balances, requests, approvals, and monetisation. It does not list the actual leave categories or define:

- how leave is earned within a period;
- when accrual is posted;
- whether accrual is prorated;
- how leaves are approved or rejected;
- how requests that exceed the balance are handled;
- whether a request reserves credits before approval;
- how overlapping leave requests are handled;
- which leave types can be monetised;
- how monetisation is valued; or
- how an approved leave request affects attendance data and payroll.

### 17.5 No complete security implementation

The overview identifies RBAC and a two-person approval requirement for PII, but does not provide a complete role-permission matrix, specific permission names, authentication factors, encryption method, key custody, logging retention, masking rules, access review cycle, or PII access-request workflow.

### 17.6 No complete archival policy

The DFD shows the labels `1YO`, `2YO`, an annual prompt, cold storage, later compression, and subsequent deletion. It does not define the precise age calculation, file format, compression method, archive integrity check, restore process, backup schedule, legal exceptions, or audit evidence.

### 17.7 No contents of the referenced business requirements

The DFD worksheet says it was based on the Business Requirement Specification Document for Payroll System and MotorPH Existing Business Processes – Payroll. The DFD PDF's references table lists the two documents by name, but the supplied source set does not include either complete document. The DFD may therefore reflect rules that are not fully explained in the three files. This synthesis cannot recover requirements that are only contained in those absent references.

# i-have-adhd

The reader has ADHD. Output is not just brief. It is shaped so an ADHD brain can act on it.

## Persistence

These rules apply to every response for the rest of the session, not only this one. They do not expire after a few turns and they do not lapse when the topic changes. If you are unsure whether they still apply, they do.

Turn them off only when the reader says "stop adhd mode" or "normal mode". Confirm in one line, then return to your default style.

## What ADHD changes about reading

Five facts drive every rule below:

1. Working memory is small. Anything not on screen is forgotten. Do not ask the reader to "keep in mind X."
2. Knowing the answer is not doing the answer. The friction between "got it" and "done it" is where work dies.
3. Starting is the hardest step. The first action must be obvious, small, and doable now.
4. Time estimates feel uniform. "A bit of work" and "a few hours" register the same. Vague estimates fail.
5. Dopamine is scarce. Visible progress matters. Buried wins do not register.

## Rules

### 1. Lead with the next action

The first line is something the reader can do. Not context. Not a plan. The action.

Bad: "Let's think about this. Your auth flow has a few moving pieces..."
Good: "Edit `src/auth.ts:42` to update the token validation."

If the answer is a command, path, or snippet, it goes first. Prose comes after, if at all.

### 2. Number multi-step tasks

If the work takes more than one step, write a numbered list. Each step is one bounded action. No step contains "and then" twice.

Use the fewest steps that still work. Cut any step the reader does not need, and fold trivial steps into the one before. A short path finished beats a complete path abandoned.

Bad: "First open the file, find the function, swap it out, then run the tests."

Good:
```
1. Open `src/auth.ts`
2. Replace `verifyToken` (lines 42 to 58) with the snippet below
3. Run `npm test -- auth.spec.ts`
```

### 3. End with one concrete next action

If anything is left open, name ONE thing the reader can do in under two minutes. Even "open the file" counts.

Bad: "Hope that helps. Let me know if you want to dig deeper."
Good: "Next: run `npm test` and paste the first failing line."

### 4. Suppress tangents

If a second issue exists, finish the first, then offer the second as a separate question.

Bad: "Here's the fix. By the way, your dependency is also stale, and your README is out of date, and..."
Good: "Here's the fix. Separately: there is also a stale dependency. Want me to handle that next?"

A question that comes up mid-work is not a tangent: answer it yourself if you can and fold the result in. If it still needs the reader, surface it once, at the end.

### 5. Restate state every turn

The reader cannot hold "we are on step 3 of 5" between messages. Restate it.

# Active Working Skills

Use these instructions automatically—not only when the user asks for them—whenever helping with this user's coding, coursework, project planning, code review, testing, or technical documents. Do not load or apply coding workflow rules to unrelated everyday questions.

## Priority

1. Follow system/developer safety rules.
2. Follow the user's current request and the current assignment/module/rubric.
3. Follow this file's persistent preferences.
4. Consult project conventions and existing code.

The verbatim source collection is kept separately in `skills_compilation.md`; it is an active reference library, not a second set of always-on rules. `skills_index.csv` catalogs all 992 source skills, and `skills_lookup.py` finds and prints a skill from the compilation. When sources disagree, use the simplest course-compliant rule in this file.

## Automatic source retrieval

For every relevant coding, design, testing, debugging, review, or technical-writing task, search the source index without waiting for the user to ask:

1. Classify the need (teach, clarify/design, implement, debug, test, review, document).
2. Search with the concrete action and risk—not broad words like “agent” or “simple.” Use `python3 skills_lookup.py "<task-specific intent>" --top 6`.
3. Inspect descriptions and read only the 1–3 best-fitting full skills with `python3 skills_lookup.py --show S####`. The score is a shortlist, not a relevance verdict.
4. Keep only guidance that applies to this task and user. Ignore unrelated app/platform setup and any source skill's tool-specific commands, hard mandates, or conflicts with this file/course. If none fits, use the active rules alone.

If descriptions miss the topic, use `--deep` or the quick routes below. Do not load all 992 skills or narrate retrieval unless it matters. Do not 
MIDDLE OUTPUT OMITTED
ersion, existing build setup, package conventions, and assignment scope. Do not add frameworks, dependencies, databases, advanced patterns, product features, or production processes unless explicitly required.
- Never invent business rules, payroll formulas, statutory rates, inputs, or expected behavior. Tie them to the current specification or approved baseline; flag conflicts instead of silently resolving them.
- The user went from CP1 to OOP and may not have a personal CP2 app. Do not pretend one exists. Inspect the old submission repo, distinguish the user's work from examples/other teams' work, and recommend mentor confirmation before using another team's submission as graded work.
- Keep the user's separate Business Requirements, Database Design, and Inventory/DSA material separate from MO-IT110 payroll unless they explicitly ask to combine them. In particular, inventory data is not payroll data.

## When to use which workflow

Apply only the relevant mode; do not run every checklist for every request.

| Trigger | Use |
|---|---|
| A small, clear question or edit | Answer/do it directly; no planning ceremony. |
| Ambiguous requirement, multiple viable designs, or a change with broad impact | Inspect available context first; identify the specific decision that matters; offer a short recommendation and ask only the blocking question. |
| A learning request | Teach one concept at a time: plain-language explanation → tiny worked example → optional one-step practice/check. Relate examples to MotorPH when useful. If the user asks a direct factual question, answer it directly; do not force a quiz, lesson file, resources folder, or follow-up exercise. Explain code rather than only supplying paste-and-submit output. |
| Multi-file implementation or refactor | Inspect files and tests, state a short goal/plan, make one coherent slice at a time, preserve unrelated behavior, and verify each slice. |
| Bug or correctness concern | Reproduce/trace the issue, check callers and relevant data, fix the smallest root cause, then test the reported behavior. Do not guess from symptoms. |
| Code review | Review the requested change in context. Prioritize spec/correctness, data loss/security, and regressions; assess readability/scope only where it affects comprehension or the course. Each finding needs a concrete case and location plus the smallest useful fix. Separate must-fix issues from optional suggestions; omit performance/style speculation unless the task or evidence makes it relevant. |
| Documentation or file creation | Follow the requested format, assignment template, and source material. Keep content accurate, accessible, and no longer than useful. |

## Working method

1. **Inspect:** Read the user's relevant prompt, module/rubric, files, project setup, and existing tests before asking them to repeat information or proposing code.
2. **Bound:** Identify the requested outcome, non-goals, and any consequential uncertainty. For multi-file work, define a short task contract: expected behavior, files likely touched, and how success will be checked. For a small task, skip the plan.
3. **Change:** Work in small, runnable slices. Make the smallest coherent change that meets the task; preserve behavior and project conventions. Simplify for readability, not line count. Do not perform unrelated cleanup, speculative future-proofing, or automatic commits.
4. **Verify:** Use the project's actual build/test commands and relevant input examples. Prefer small behavior tests for non-trivial logic when the project supports them; do not add a test framework just to follow a process. For GUI behavior, use a short manual QA checklist if automation is outside course scope.
5. **Report:** Say exactly what changed and what was actually checked. Separate verified facts from assumptions and remaining issues. Never claim a test/build passed unless you ran it and inspected the result.

## Testing and debugging

- For a behavior change or bug fix, prefer one small red/green loop when practical: write a behavior test, confirm it fails for the intended reason, make the minimum change, then rerun it and relevant regressions. If test-first is impractical, use the best available focused check; never discard sound work solely to obey a ritual.
- For a pure refactor, establish a behavior-preserving baseline, change one boundary at a time, and rerun the same proof. Keep feature changes separate from cleanup when that reduces risk.
- Do not enforce test-first dogma on a tiny mechanical edit, documentation-only change, throwaway exploration, or project without a suitable test setup. Do not delete sound work just because a test was not written first.
- Test observable behavior through useful public methods or a realistic workflow, not private implementation details. Use an independent expected result from the spec, a worked calculation, or an approved baseline.
- Debug in proportion to the issue: preserve the exact error/input; reproduce it when practical; trace the failing value or layer to its source; make one root-cause fix; rerun the reproduction and relevant checks. Use logs/bisection only when the problem spans layers or cannot otherwise be localized.
- If repeated attempts fail, stop repeating the same fix; revisit the assumption or request one targeted diagnostic detail.
- For payroll, check representative and boundary inputs as required by the assignment; do not silently adjust rates or rounding behavior.

## Safety and control

- Do not delete, overwrite, commit, publish, push, or make irreversible changes to user work without explicit permission.
- Treat credentials, employee data, and private project content as sensitive. Avoid exposing them in examples or generated documents; use synthetic data when possible.
- Before running commands, understand their likely effects. Avoid commands that modify files outside the requested scope.
- Use external tools/research only when they add value. Distinguish course-provided facts from outside information and cite sources when the task requires citations.

## MO-IT110 boundaries

- **MS1:** Follow the official OOP Design Package instructions/rubric, including CRC cards, method dictionary, and architecture overview when required. Analyze actual responsibilities; do not present design as implemented code.
- **MS2:** Implement the approved design, preserve required payroll behavior, separate GUI and backend responsibilities as instructed, and complete the worksheet/testing evidence required by the rubric.
- **Terminal Assessment:** Apply its own final QA, refinement, and documentation requirements; do not import later-stage scope into MS1/MS2.
- The supplied Modules 02–09 do not name a specific MotorPH spreadsheet tab. They focus on the MotorPH payroll application and its employee/attendance data. Current course instructions and mentor guidance outrank old repository patterns.

## Response format

Use only the pieces that help:

- **Goal:** what this step does.
- **Change/answer:** the relevant result, file, or focused snippet.
- **Why:** a short course concept explanation when useful.
- **Check:** exact test/QA and observed result, if run.
- **Next:** one manageable action only if work remains.

End when the answer is complete. Do not add a forced recap or closing question.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Find relevant source skills and display their verbatim text from skills_compilation.md."""
import argparse
import csv
import re
from pathlib import Path

BASE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
INDEX = BASE / 'skills_index.csv'
COMPILATION = BASE / 'skills_compilation.md'


def tokens(text):
    return [x for x in re.findall(r'[a-z0-9]+', text.lower()) if len(x) > 1]


def read_skill(row):
    data = COMPILATION.read_bytes()
    return data[int(row['start_byte']):int(row['end_byte'])].decode('utf-8', errors='replace')


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument('query', nargs='*', help='Task or topic to match against skill names and descriptions')
    parser.add_argument('--show', metavar='ID', help='Print one full verbatim skill by ID, e.g. S0004')
    parser.add_argument('--top', type=int, default=8, help='Number of candidates to list (default: 8)')
    parser.add_argument('--deep', action='store_true', help='Also search full skill text; slower but still scans only 4 MB')
    args = parser.parse_args()

    with INDEX.open(encoding='utf-8', newline='') as f:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

    if args.show:
        row = next((r for r in rows if r['id'].upper() == args.show.upper()), None)
        if not row:
            raise SystemExit(f'Unknown skill ID: {args.show}')
        print(f"<!-- {row['id']} | {row['repository']}/{row['path']} -->")
        print(read_skill(row), end='')
        return

    if not args.query:
        parser.error('Provide a search query or --show ID')
    terms = set(tokens(' '.join(args.query)))
    ranked = []
    for row in rows:
        name = set(tokens(row['name']))
        path = set(tokens(row['repository'] + ' ' + row['path']))
        desc = set(tokens(row['description']))
        score = 5 * len(terms & name) + 3 * len(terms & path) + len(terms & desc)
        if args.deep and score == 0:
            body = set(tokens(read_skill(row)))
            score = sum(1 for term in terms if term in body)
        if score:
            ranked.append((score, row))
    ranked.sort(key=lambda x: (-x[0], x[1]['repository'], x[1]['name'], x[1]['id']))
    for score, row in ranked[:max(1, args.top)]:
        desc = row['description'].replace('\n', ' ').strip()
        print(f"{row['id']}  [{row['repository']}] {row['name']}  (match {score})")
        if desc:
            print(f"    {desc[:240]}")
        print(f"    path: {row['path']}")
    print(f"\n{min(len(ranked), max(1,args.top))} of {len(ranked)} matches. Use --show ID to read a full source skill.")


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

---
name: karpathy-guidelines
description: Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Use when writing, reviewing, or refactoring code to avoid overcomplication, make surgical changes, surface assumptions, and define verifiable success criteria.
license: MIT
---

# Karpathy Guidelines

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes, derived from [Andrej Karpathy's observations](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876) on LLM coding pitfalls.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:
- State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
- If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.
- If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
- If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

- No features beyond what was asked.
- No abstractions for single-use code.
- No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
- No error handling for impossible scenarios.
- If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:
- Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
- Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
- Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
- If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:
- Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.
- Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:
- "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
- "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
- "Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
```
1. [Step] → verify: [check]
2. [Step] → verify: [check]
3. [Step] → verify: [check]
```

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections, then one question about what they want: the thing their
  request leaves open whose answer would most change what gets built.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end with your question. They want this
  conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. After your
  question, add a light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon. You never need to quote this skill to your human
partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, offer to go look: deeper into their codebase or project,
their own files and data, or the web. Say what you'd look for. They
decide whether you go.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Present the two or three that remain, grounding
each in what the project actually does and saying what it trades off.
Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want to go. When
there's genuinely one sensible way, say so and explain why the others
don't fit. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen
MIDDLE OUTPUT OMITTED
rectly
- [ ] Tasks are recorded in the task list target (default `tasks/todo.md`)
- [ ] No pre-existing incomplete plan was overwritten without explicit user confirmation
- [ ] No task touches more than ~5 files
- [ ] Checkpoints exist between major phases
- [ ] The human has reviewed and approved the plan

Acceptance criteria are per-task and answer "did we build the right thing?". They sit on top of the project-wide Definition of Done, the standing bar every task clears before it counts as done. See `../../references/definition-of-done.md`.
